stories.title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
stories.titleZh: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
stories.author: zulln
summaryZh: Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.What caused the ground stopTransportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.Why disruptions continued SaturdayAirlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.02:31Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers.Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.02:41Nationwide ground stops are extremely rareGround stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

stories.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
stories.titleZh: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
stories.author: jcubic
summaryZh: This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.See hacker news for discussion

comments.author: jrmg
comments.textZhHtml:
In the United States the Copyright Office actually has guidance on this that I feel most people aren’t aware of.

https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intell...

An excerpt, with emphasis mine:

• Questions of copyrightability and AI can be resolved pursuant to existing law, without the need for legislative change.

• The use of AI tools to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect the availability of copyright protection for the output.

• Copyright protects the original expression in a work created by a human author, even if the work also includes AI-generated material.

• Copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements.

• Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.

• Based on the functioning of current generally available technology, prompts do not alone provide sufficient control.

• Human authors are entitled to copyright in their works of authorship that are perceptible in AI-generated outputs, as well as the creative selection, coordination, or arrangement of material in the outputs, or creative modifications of the outputs.

• The case has not been made for additional copyright or sui generis protection for AI- generated content.

I am sure there will be many more legal battles and probably legislation about this to come.

stories.titleZh: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
stories.author: speckx
summaryZh: Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions. The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

comments.author: Silfen
comments.textZhHtml:
Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why Nvidia would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding.

Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means Nvidia takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips.

Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

summaryZh: November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink>) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort: a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido

stories.titleZh: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
stories.author: armcat
summaryZh: Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive DataAI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.Diesen Artikel auf Deutsch lesenAbout LovableLovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience.Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.Visit the Lovable websiteThe PromiseLovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?In its marketing, Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects. This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German).Research QuestionWe wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.MethodologyWe focused on the database service Supabase. Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl, we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).LimitationsEmail addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.Data LeaksWe found many serious cases of exposed data, including:A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details, including passport numbers, expiration dates, and nationalities. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts, invoices, personal photo albums, and internal WhatsApp communications.We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider’s customers were accessible.Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.ImplicationsOur analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment.Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026.Get in touch for an informal conversation. We'll look at your current situation and work with you to find the right solutions.Contact an expert

We might be the same generation, I recognize the two roles. What I also remember is just empirically how much better the "programmers" were at doing the "system analysts" job. Way, way better. Then we stopped educating system analysts and now the job title is not heard of anymore.

I regularly meet (recently examined) people who are trained "software architects". Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project. The best programmers are just so much better software architects also. So I expect history to repeat at this point.

comments.author: EarthBlues
comments.textZhHtml:
Programmers are better architects because their decisions are continually informed by experience from the "sharp end" of the system.  LLMs don't really have experiences, I dont think its the same.
Our profession will likely shake out a lot of people in the coming years.  What will be left may not be a classic "systems analyst" or "architect" role. I think the people who stay in this field will have to move both up and down the abstraction stack simultaneously -- our job will become a lot more "real", physical, relational, risk-oriented.  I dont think there's good reason to believe LLMs can supply the need for prudence in the fields where software is deployed.

comments.author: ctkhn
comments.textZhHtml: You do need to stay in touch with the sharp end to stay sharp yourself. I've had a lot of managers and directors in my career who as they have moved up in companies, longer write any code, and seem to not really get how our systems work even though they are in charge. I had a few managers in the past who were "non technical" and had never written code in their life, and they were the absolute worst of the bunch. There is a little bit of truth to the otherwise very corny comic with the guy with an enormous head saying "at the library" when asked where he works out. https://i.pinimg.com/736x/3c/69/3a/3c693a6f9e3f6949192ce613e...

comments.author: saltcured
comments.textZhHtml:
In my opinion, a lot of that "no longer getting it" is because of the social/fashion trends that continually disrupt programming.

You don't forget CS concepts so easily, but all the syntactic tricks of new language variants and working set vocabulary of APIs, data formats, and frameworks keeps churning away from whatever you last had contacted in a real, hands-on way.

It is fascinating, wondering where this is going as programmers turn into their own middle managers on top of agents. Particularly, the school who claim that you don't really need to understand all the code and instead treat it like a black-box experiment. If this fad takes over the main stage, then everyone becomes one of those less technical managers.

But, in this new scenario, there is no human in the loop to inject judgement calls and "manage up" anymore. There is no programmer culture except the models and agents, which don't really have the same social connections to drive a programming culture. What will happen? A culture per agent product? Per enterprise client of the agent vendor? Per agent operator? Per codebase?

comments.author: ohyes
comments.textZhHtml: I don’t think we get new things. Right now they’re great at popular languages and frameworks. If those change? There’s not enough training data. It could generate the data and train itself but where’s the incentive. It certainly can’t learn a new language right away the way even a junior programmer can. It will constantly hallucinate and not improve.

comments.author: torginus
comments.textZhHtml:
Weird how these fads just disappear overnight, 1984 style.

About half a year ago I noticed there were no people called 'Agile something' at our org, so I asked about it. They looked at me like I was a space alien. I remember, it was like 3 years ago that management bet the house on 'Agile transformation' talking about how Agile practices are the bread and butter of a good organization.

Now they're talking about AI the same way.

comments.author: ctkhn
comments.textZhHtml: To be fair there is something to the idea of moving to agile from waterfall practices, the same way going on any diet in general makes you think about what you're eating and helps you lose weight. Unfortunately it's usually just a way for the same management (who have fostered bad practices) to hire a new set of consultants and look like they're doing something without actually fixing anything.

comments.author: torginus
comments.textZhHtml: Yes, that something is about moving from a management class composed mostly of senior engineers to Agile cultists whose core tenet is that they do not know anything about engineering, and do not wish to, because as long as the principles of Agile are followed correctly, it doesn't matter if your company makes software or matresses.

comments.author: somesortofthing
comments.textZhHtml: "Don't try to completely plan out huge software projects and commit to rigid delivery timelines in advance," "Split work into manageable tasks", "Run daily meetings to keep managers(and sometimes coworkers) in the decision loop and surface blockers", etc. are iron laws everyone instinctively recognizes are there for a reason. The explicit framework fell away because its principles became ubiquitous - nobody needs to hire Agile™ consultants to tell their SWEs and managers to do things the way they've been doing them for their whole career.

comments.author: ElevenLathe
comments.textZhHtml:
You say this like its universal, but my ostensibly Agile org is currently planning the work we will be delivering Q1 of 2028 because that is how long our [proposed work] -> [approved work] -> [finished work] pipeline runs.

The memo has NOT gotten around, though AI now makes it easier to make all the various slide decks and schedule all the 50+ person meetings that power this process.

comments.author: fcarraldo
comments.textZhHtml: Sounds like Scaled Agile Framework aka SAFe or something similar? A total consulting scam sold to clueless execs (I worked for some, these processes are a nightmare)

comments.author: ahartmetz
comments.textZhHtml: It's fun to remind people of past hypes and how they disappeared. Some don't seem to get the connection to the current thing. (Note, I'm not saying AI is nothing.)

comments.author: derefr
comments.textZhHtml:
> Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project.

Negative value to the project, perhaps; but if these "software architects" are kept around despite several rounds of this, it may be because they're providing positive value to the company, in terms of producing for the company a thing whose existence (no matter how flawed) serves as collateral for:

- the executive team, to show to investors, to convince them that they're acting strategically in the market; or

- the marketing team, to get breathless puff-piece articles written about the company, in places where dumb CTOs/CIOs who make IT buying decisions will read them. (Not necessarily to then buy the specific product that came out of that project — hopefully not, in fact! — but instead to remember the company itself the next time they're comparing vendors for something else);

- or the executive team again, this time to show to a potential acquirer, to convince the acquirer that their employees have a higher asset value for having a certain skill / experience with certain paradigms, that they gained working on this project.

Companies have spent collective billions (trillions?) of dollars on projects they know will go nowhere, just to be able to say they did a project that is made a certain way or does a certain thing or has certain certifications, and to have a shitty codebase they can pull out of their back pocket if needed to back that up. In all such cases, even if they need to present the product, the product will never be evaluated for its quality or for its fit-for-purpose-ness; so it doesn't matter that the project failed to produce something of quality or that is fit-for-purpose. It just matters that the project happened.

comments.author: microtonal
comments.textZhHtml:
The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

I think both definitions are still too narrow for what I do daily. I fully agree that we still need humans to decide what to build, how it should all fit together, etc.

But both definitions do not really take into account the huge social dimension of being a good (computer) engineer in a company. You have to translate requests from a wild variety of users into what this means for a system. You have to recognize and explain that what they need is not always what they think they need. You have to be able to say "no" to things. All these things are very hard for an LLM (reading humans, not literally following requests).

Then there are social aspects like building consensus within a project, building a user base of many people that are initially skeptical, using existing relations with people and other companies to slowly adopt what you are building, etc.

Programming used to be a large chunk of the work. I thoroughly enjoyed this aspect of the work when I was younger, but at some point I started enjoying system design and everything around it more. So in that sense, programming with LLMs is much nicer (though I still review every single line of code and often have to go through a couple of iterations because even Opus 5.5 often doesn't get it 'right' in the first take). But the remaining part of the work is extremely hard for an LLM to replace.

comments.author: parasti
comments.textZhHtml:
> You have to be able to say "no" to things.

How do you justify saying "no" when there is a magic machine invented 3 years ago that'll do it? Your gut says it's a maintenance nightmare, your LLM says it's already done implementing it.

comments.author: prmph
comments.textZhHtml:
Then we have/had "Software Engineer", then "Software Architect", etc.

Words are just words. In tech especially, it seems anyone can call themselves whatever they want.

Someone who chooses to call themselves "programmer" can be more engineering-minded and see the big picture better than someone that calls themselves an engineer.

comments.author: retwakm4
comments.textZhHtml:
I prefer to call myself a programmer because I don't think we (as a class) consistently perform a lot of the types of duties (both ethical ones and just basic job performance ones) that would be required of a lot of engineering disciplines.

I also started out in systems programming and we still call ourselves programmers there, when there is a lot of systems "engineering" (aka trying not to blow up the system with your code running in supervisor state) going on. And there, a lot more attention paid to stuff like IEEE code of ethics, professional development, rigorous designs, etc.

So I'll keep to calling myself programmer amongst my non software engineering friends. It just seems more humble.

That being said, writing the code has like others have pointed out, never been the largest part of the job in my experience. So I can see how it may be confusing to some, especially software engineers. But to non software engineers I think they mostly get it...you are a software engineer trying not to imply some some sort of unearned intellectual superiority.

comments.author: ModernMech
comments.textZhHtml: It's not about what people call themselves, it appears there are actually distinct roles here, and AI is automating only one of them (for now).

comments.author: literallyanythi
comments.textZhHtml:
Scrolled down the page, saw this "Very Easy" 1 minute plane

https://www.foldableflight.com/planes/mystic

Started watching the video not planning on actually making it, saw that it is done with A4 paper and grabbed a random sheet at my desk to follow along. The pocket felt like a nice "a-ha!" moment. As someone who only knew the "naive" way to make paper airplanes from A4 paper, this is the best performing and prettiest paper airplane I've made in my life! It almost feels like it's not real how smoothly it stays straight in the air compared to all my paper airplanes in childhood.

Edit: Tried making the flapping wings AeroDactyl but it didn't work out :( wasn't aerodynamic and didn't flap its wings just went straight to the ground

Edit 2: Tried making the Jetstream (another 1 minute plane) and it came out well! Mine is INCREDIBLY asymmetrical and still flies better than any other plane I've made other than the Mystic!

Edit 3: Tried making the Advanced Elanus and I made it! But it's a little shoddy and much tougher for sure. Looks cool but it doesn't glide anywhere near as good as in the video (I guess you really need to perfect it.)

Final edit: My planes :) https://i.imgur.com/xnMdzJv.jpeg

comments.author: bronco21016
comments.textZhHtml: I've been making the original version of this, the Nakamura Lock, since seeing it in a book as a child. I messed with tons of "world record distance" designs as a kid but this design just always came out the most consistent and had great performance. My favorite part is just the simplicity of it.

comments.author: dotancohen
comments.textZhHtml:
> I messed with tons of "world record distance" designs as a kid
In seventh or right grade we had a paper airplane contest. I literally walked up to the throwing line holding an unfolded piece of paper. At the line I crumbled it up, it flew straighter and faster then any other airplane thrown that day, and I think only one or two airplanes beat it for distance. My appeal at being disqualified was rejected, though I broke no rules.

comments.author: johncoltrane
comments.textZhHtml:
When my daughter and niece were 11 and 9, we had a paper airplane folding afternoon. We went through the handful of designs I remembered from middle school with some level of success. All along, I was teasing them about a super plane I knew how to make.I eventually made it and it flew so much better than all the other ones… but they hated me for it.

It turned out that they wanted paper planes that conformed to their idea of a paper plane, not paper-based engineering marvels.

Apparently, that design is called "two loops".

comments.author: chrismorgan
comments.textZhHtml:
I’ve pulled that trick multiple times, normally successfully; some people appreciate such shenanigans.

A similar anecdote. There was once a bridge-building competition, with provided materials, and scores for it bearing different weight toy cars, for height and for length. Nowhere was it said the bridge had to bear any of the cars. Our group’s 15-metre long roll of tape bridge with four-pop-stick-A-frame supports, which scored three times as much as the next (… and we could have doubled its length), was unceremoniously disqualified for unspecified grounds, as I had expected. I pressed for a few days for the grounds (even suggesting the couple of not-unreasonable grounds I had thought of, such as that our team had schismed into two over the creative direction), but was not given them.

The unwritten rules about spirit can be applied capriciously.

I think ours was still the most popular bridge. And honestly one of the more realistic, just scaled for much smaller vehicles, a consistent 1:500 where most were an inconsistent 1:25 to 1:50. They were really good supports.

comments.author: fweimer
comments.textZhHtml:
Well, OpenOffice wouldn't print on Tuesdays:

“ What a fascinating bug!! My wife has complained that open office will never print on Tuesdays!?! Then she demonstrated it. Sure enough, won't print on Tuesday. Other applications print. I think this is the same bug. Here is my guess:

Print to a postscript file. Observe the line: %%CreationDate: (Tue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Change "Tue" to anything else: %%CreationDate: (XTue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Save the file and it prints. Tools like evince work because they simply omit the "CreationDate" tag to begin with.

Now something odd happens when my cups script (I am using the Brother MFC420CN) copies the file to a temp file. Some of the code is rearranged, not sure how or why, but it uses a command called "file" to identify the file as "PostScript". This check would work on the original file you printed, but by the time it runs the check on the temp file, it misidentifies. Normally it would return:

   PostScript document text conforming at level 3.0
But there is another check that happens before the PostScript check. If it finds "Tue" at the fourth byte of the file, it identifies it as:

   Jan 22 14:32:44 MET 1991\011Erlang JAM file - version 4.2
So it's not a problem w/ openoffice.org, cups, or the brother printer drivers. It is a bug in the `file` utility, and documented at https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/file/+bug/248619. ”

https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/cupsys/+bug/255161...

comments.textZhHtml:
I'm having trouble understanding your question in the context of the discussion, so I will talk about the topic generally instead.

Imagine a server allows you to upload images. It has a system designed for images only. It will behave unpredictably maybe even dangerously with another file. The server checks that the file ends with .jpg. it checks that the file is a valid jpeg. All clear. Upload allowed. But 5 steps later some tool looks at the image file and notices it's a valid zip file (creating files with multiple valid interpretations is something people have succeeded in doing it's not always so hard). It runs this check before the image check. The next step in the processing chain wants an image but it has been told it's dealing with a zip file. So it unzips the file to see if it contains an image. But it was a zip bomb. The server goes down.

That's not how a printer with a fax/modem works.

If the printer endpoint of the USB device receives a file that orders millions of pizzas, it will print the file (or print a PS error, or print the plaintext contents of the file), not order pizzas.

If the user mistakenly "prints" to the fax device, the file will be printed at the destination fax machine, at the number the user typed, not the number in the file, and it will print, not order pizzas (unless the pizzeria accepts fax orders, which would be a prank, not an attack).

comments.author: smugglerFlynn
comments.textZhHtml:
Replacing a good app is still extremely hard. Let me explain.

Commodities like todo apps and calculators rarely compete on features, they compete on product design. This includes look and feel, relation between elements, design choices on what exact common features are available.

All products are, at their essence, just a set of design decisions stitched and shipped together.

Now, making these design decisions is hard. It requires knowledge, consistency, and insights into how real people operate real products. Even as a sole user of the app you build you rarely know what you actually need.

LLMs are 'design-less' in their essence. Building your own todo app takes literal seconds and it all looks simple because LLMs will default most of these design decisions for you - until you try to use your new app daily and notice it somehow sucks. Building a good todo app or good calculator requires tweaking, publishing, polishing, and solving bugs, testing, rinse and repeat.

Another tricky side of this is that you might know logically what features you want, but you are not selecting one product over another logically. You need to try and see if that works for you, all the vibes and good parts and bad parts and design choices and colors, till you find something that "clicks" for you. Using pure Claude as a todo app only works as long as you want to have more Claude in your daily life.

In the meantime app store provides dozens of well-reviewed alternative solutions which look good and require zero maintenance.

And that's just a calculator or todo app. Non-commodity apps are even harder than that.
